paragraphs: Answering questions about long documents requires finding evidence across text, images, and tables, then combining it into a coherent answer. Text-centered retrieval can overlook visual evidence even when that evidence is essential. This paper introduces MMDocRAG to evaluate how systems handle the full process of retrieving, selecting, and integrating information across document formats and pages.

The benchmark contains 4,055 expert-annotated question-answer pairs with evidence chains spanning multiple pages and modalities. Its evaluation framework includes metrics for selecting multimodal quotations and supports answers that combine written explanations with relevant visual elements. This makes evidence selection itself an explicit evaluation target, alongside the resulting answer.

Experiments cover 60 vision-language or language models and 14 retrieval systems. Proprietary models perform better overall and gain moderately from multimodal inputs, while open-source alternatives suffer substantial degradation with those inputs. Fine-tuned language models improve substantially when given detailed image descriptions. These findings show that access to images alone does not ensure effective document reasoning; how systems represent and integrate visual evidence matters.
neurips-2025-benchmarking-retrieval-augm.tldr: MMDocRAG benchmarks document question answering across text and visuals, revealing persistent weaknesses in retrieving and integrating multimodal evidence.

paragraphs: A classification system may receive several observations of the same instance, such as multiple photographs of one plant. Those images provide complementary evidence, but combining them should also preserve reliable uncertainty estimates. This paper adapts conformal prediction to that setting, producing a set of plausible labels while maintaining the required coverage guarantee separately for each class.

The method computes conformal p-values from each observation and then aggregates them. Its central ingredient is the exact distribution of those p-values, which supports a general framework for combining evidence through a scoring function. The framework accommodates many classical statistical tools and also enables refined versions of familiar approaches such as majority voting.

Using the extra observations can reduce the number of labels returned without sacrificing the stated class-conditional coverage. The authors evaluate the method on simulated and real data, with particular attention to plant identification through Pl@ntNet. The contribution connects a practical prediction setting with a statistical guarantee: multiple images can sharpen the answer while retaining uncertainty protection at the class level.
neurips-2025-class-conditional-conformal.tldr: Aggregating conformal p-values from multiple observations can produce smaller prediction sets while preserving class-conditional coverage.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can be adapted by rewarding desirable outputs or by combining pretrained models that emphasize different properties. Both approaches become difficult when those properties compete. Improving one objective can undermine another, and existing methods do not guarantee that the resulting model faithfully captures every desired property.

This paper places alignment and composition within one constrained optimization framework. For alignment, the model must satisfy reward constraints. For composition, it can be required to remain close to each contributing pretrained model. The framework can also combine these requirements. This formulation makes competing demands explicit instead of leaving their balance entirely implicit in an optimization objective.

The authors theoretically characterize solutions to these constrained problems and develop a Lagrangian primal-dual training algorithm that approximates them. Image-generation experiments demonstrate both alignment and composition, with the resulting models effectively satisfying the imposed constraints. The findings support constrained learning as a practical way to manage competing requirements, while the algorithm's approximate nature remains distinct from the theoretical characterization of the solutions.
neurips-2025-composition-and-alignment-o.tldr: A constrained learning framework unifies diffusion-model alignment and composition, with an approximate training algorithm that effectively satisfies constraints in image-generation experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops diffusion models that operate in representation spaces of Lie groups, mathematical structures used to describe transformations. The approach allows the transformation structure to shape generation directly. Its framework includes non-Abelian groups, where the order of transformations matters, and recovers ordinary score matching when the chosen group describes translations.

Using generalized score matching, the authors derive Langevin dynamics that split into components corresponding to Lie algebra representations. They also prove that the generative processes solve a new class of paired stochastic differential equations. The theoretical framework supports modeling any target distribution on any non-Abelian Lie group, giving the construction broad scope beyond a single application.

Experiments include rotation-guided molecular conformer generation using SO(3) and ligand-specific rigid transformations using SE(3) for molecular docking. The approach improves on Riemannian diffusion performed on the group itself in these applications. The authors further show that an appropriate group choice can reduce the effective dimensionality of generation trajectories, improve learning efficiency, and support transitions between complex distributions.
neurips-2025-diffusion-generative-modeli.tldr: Diffusion in Lie-group representation spaces provides a general transformation-aware framework and improves molecular generation and docking results over diffusion on the group itself.

paragraphs: Gene expression measurements can show two genes varying together without one regulating the other. Hidden factors can create these associations, but so can observing only cells that survive or meet inclusion criteria. This paper argues that the latter mechanism, selection bias, is widespread and often overlooked, potentially distorting inferred regulatory networks and recommendations for intervention.

The authors use gene perturbations to distinguish these mechanisms. Their key observation is that dependencies induced by selection behave symmetrically under perturbation, whereas dependencies arising from regulation or confounding do not. This difference supplies information that observational associations alone cannot provide and motivates a method that explicitly separates regulatory and non-regulatory explanations.

The resulting algorithm, GISL, uses perturbation data to recover gene regulatory relations together with mechanisms of selection and hidden confounding. Recovery is up to an equivalence class, meaning the method can leave multiple explanations indistinguishable rather than always identifying one unique network. Experiments on synthetic and real gene expression data support its effectiveness in handling these competing sources of dependence.
neurips-2025-gene-regulatory-network-inf.tldr: GISL uses gene perturbations to distinguish regulation, hidden confounding, and selection effects, recovering their structure up to an equivalence class.

paragraphs: Rendering a scene from new viewpoints requires representing both its geometry and how its appearance changes with viewing direction. Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting achieves high quality at real-time speeds, but storing many properties for every Gaussian consumes substantial memory. Compressing those properties into neural fields can lose rapidly changing spatial details and damage fine reconstruction.

HyRF divides the representation according to what needs explicit storage. A compact collection of Gaussians retains critical high-frequency parameters, while grid-based neural fields predict the remaining properties. Separate neural fields handle geometry and view-dependent color, allowing those components to be modeled independently. A hybrid renderer also combines Gaussian splatting with a predicted background to better represent distant parts of the scene.

The experiments report state-of-the-art rendering quality, a model more than 20 times smaller than 3D Gaussian Splatting, and continued real-time performance. The result supports a selective approach to compression: retain explicit detail where it matters most, and use learned fields to represent the remaining scene properties compactly.
neurips-2025-hyrf-hybrid-radiance-fields.tldr: HyRF combines explicit Gaussians with neural fields to deliver state-of-the-art rendering quality at over 20 times smaller model size than 3DGS while remaining real-time.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate impressive images but struggle to follow editing instructions that substantially change an existing image's layout. Such edits require more than preserving a scene while modifying its appearance. This paper identifies structurally inconsistent editing as a central difficulty and proposes breaking complicated instructions into a sequence of manageable operations.

Image Editing As Programs, or IEAP, builds this approach on a Diffusion Transformer architecture. Each atomic operation handles a particular kind of structurally consistent edit. Executing these operations in sequence allows the framework to compose transformations that can be structurally inconsistent overall. The organizing principle is that a difficult global change can be expressed through a program of simpler editing steps.

Experiments on standard benchmarks show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across multiple editing scenarios. The reported gains include editing accuracy and semantic fidelity, especially for complex instructions requiring several steps. These findings support programmatic decomposition as a way to improve instruction following across both structure-preserving edits and edits involving substantial layout changes.
neurips-2025-image-editing-as-programs-w.tldr: IEAP decomposes image-editing instructions into atomic operations, improving accuracy and semantic fidelity for complex edits, including major layout changes.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models learn to recover data from corrupted versions, but interpreting their training losses as probability estimates requires a theoretical connection. This paper develops that connection through information theory. It relates how much information corrupted data retains about the original to the best achievable denoising loss.

The authors derive an Information–Minimum Denoising Score Entropy relation for discrete diffusion and a corresponding cross-entropy relation for masked diffusion. These identities express data log-likelihood through an integral of optimal score-based losses over diffusion time. At those optima, the relationship is tight, giving the losses a likelihood interpretation beyond serving merely as variational bounds.

For masked diffusion, the decomposition also supports a time-free formula, conditional likelihood estimation for prompt-response tasks, and coupled Monte Carlo estimates of likelihood ratios. These extensions turn the theoretical identities into tools for evaluating probabilities and comparing them. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the estimators' accuracy, variance stability, and practical usefulness, connecting the optimal-loss theory to empirical estimation.
neurips-2025-information-theoretic-discr.tldr: Information-theoretic identities connect optimal discrete diffusion losses to exact log-likelihood decompositions and enable practical likelihood estimators.

paragraphs: Mean-field games describe interactions among an infinite population of agents. Finding an equilibrium means finding policies consistent with that population's behavior. Existing algorithms can require strict monotonicity or guarantee convergence only after averaging many successive policies. This paper studies whether the latest policy itself can converge under the weaker condition of non-strict monotonicity.

The authors prove that a proximal-point update with KL regularization has this last-iterate convergence property. They then show that each update amounts to solving a KL-regularized mean-field game. Mirror descent can find the equilibrium of that regularized problem with an exponential last-iterate convergence rate, providing a way to implement the update through an inner optimization procedure.

Their Approximate Proximal-Point algorithm, APP, uses a small number of mirror descent steps to approximate each proximal update. Benchmark experiments show reliable convergence to the original, unregularized equilibrium without time averaging. The exponential rate concerns the regularized inner problem; the broader contribution is convergence of the current policy under non-strict monotonicity and a practical approximation supported by numerical results.
neurips-2025-last-iterate-convergence-in.tldr: KL-regularized proximal updates achieve last-policy convergence under non-strict monotonicity, and APP approximates them using a few mirror descent steps.

paragraphs: Combining several data sources can improve clustering, but many methods need some known matches between observations across sources. Fully incomplete multi-view clustering removes those correspondences entirely. This paper addresses that setting by matching the higher-level category structures found in different views, rather than trying to begin with paired individual examples.

The Contrastive Prototype Matching Network first uses graph contrastive learning and mutual nearest-neighbor relationships to discover structure within entirely unpaired views. It builds initial cluster prototypes from that structure, then matches graphs of prototypes across views. This step resolves category misalignment and creates a common clustering structure without requiring initial instance correspondences.

A final prototype-aware contrastive learning stage uses the alignment to encourage semantic consistency. It replaces reliance on the initial neighbor-based structural similarities with guidance from the matched categories. Benchmark experiments show significant improvements over multiple baselines and ablation variants. The findings support the paper's central choice: shared category structure can provide a useful basis for connecting views when individual observations are unpaired.
neurips-2025-learning-from-disjoint-view.tldr: CPMN clusters completely unpaired data views by aligning category prototypes and using that alignment to guide contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Operating-system agents use screenshots to understand a computer interface and then act through APIs that control inputs such as clicks and keystrokes. This connects visual interpretation directly to actions on a user's machine. The paper investigates how manipulating a small visible region can redirect that behavior even while the agent is carrying out a legitimate task.

The attack uses Malicious Image Patches: adversarially modified screen regions that induce harmful actions through particular APIs when the agent captures them. The authors describe placements such as desktop wallpaper or social-media content and identify sensitive-data exfiltration as a possible consequence. The attack therefore reaches the agent through material it sees during normal interaction.

The study shows that these patches generalize across user prompts and screen configurations and can hijack multiple operating-system agents during benign instructions. This broadens the finding beyond one fixed screenshot or task. The security implication is that an agent's visual inputs can become a route to unauthorized computer actions, making the connection between perception and API execution a consequential vulnerability.
neurips-2025-mip-against-agent-malicious.tldr: Malicious image patches can redirect screenshot-driven computer agents into harmful API actions across different prompts and screen configurations.

paragraphs: Optimizing the latent inputs of a text-to-image model can benefit from keeping those inputs consistent with a standard Gaussian distribution. This paper introduces a regularization loss that encourages that consistency. It treats the entries of a high-dimensional sample as one-dimensional Gaussian variables and checks their statistical properties in two complementary ways.

One component matches moments in the spatial domain; another matches power-spectrum properties in the spectral domain. Their expected Gaussian values are known analytically, providing targets for the loss. Applying the losses to randomly permuted inputs provides permutation invariance. The framework also unifies earlier regularizers: some are particular moment losses, while an earlier covariance-matching loss is equivalent to the spectral component but more costly to compute.

The authors apply the regularizer to test-time reward alignment for aesthetics and text agreement in image generation. In that application, it outperforms previous Gaussianity regularization, prevents reward hacking, and speeds convergence. The results connect the statistical construction to a practical objective: improving rewarded image properties while controlling departures from the intended latent distribution.
neurips-2025-moment-and-power-spectrum-b.tldr: A combined moment and power-spectrum loss improves Gaussianity regularization, preventing reward hacking and accelerating convergence in demonstrated image-alignment tasks.

paragraphs: Text watermarks insert statistical signals into generated language so that its origin can later be checked. Many detectors use statistics that are independent and identically distributed under human-written text. Goodness-of-fit tests can examine whether observed statistics depart from that expected distribution, making them natural candidates for detecting watermark signals.

This paper systematically evaluates eight such tests across three watermarking schemes. The study uses three open-source language models, two datasets, different generation temperatures, and several post-editing methods. This design examines both detection power and robustness across multiple conditions, rather than judging a statistical test in a single watermarking configuration.

The results show that general goodness-of-fit tests can improve detection and resistance to post-editing. The authors also identify a particular advantage associated with repeated text, which is common at low generation temperatures and is not exploited by existing methods. These are empirical findings across the evaluated settings. They support revisiting classical statistical tests as simple tools for strengthening watermark detection, including conditions where generation behavior creates useful additional signals.
neurips-2025-on-the-empirical-power-of-g.tldr: An empirical study finds that classical goodness-of-fit tests can improve watermark detection power and robustness, including by exploiting repeated text.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the idea that AI innovation and regulation necessarily pull in opposite directions. It argues that failures in consequential AI systems already produce social, economic, and democratic harm. Drawing on analogies with aviation, pharmaceuticals, and welfare systems, the authors frame thoughtful, adaptable regulation as a foundation for responsible technological progress.

The paper examines the EU AI Act as a model for governing systems according to risk and responsibility. Its discussion centers on the difficulty of intervening early enough to prevent harm while remaining flexible as technology develops. Regulatory sandboxes, support for smaller enterprises, real-world testing, and fundamental-rights impact assessments illustrate the mechanisms the authors believe can address that tension.

The proposed benefits include clearer legal expectations, stronger consumer trust, and competitiveness grounded in ethical practice. These are elements of the paper's argument about governance, rather than experimental findings. Its central position is that transparency, accountability, impact assessment, and AI literacy should be built into development and deployment, with fundamental rights helping define what counts as successful innovation.
neurips-2025-position-if-innovation-in-a.tldr: This position paper argues that adaptive, rights-centered regulation can enable responsible AI innovation, using the EU AI Act as its principal example.

paragraphs: Quantum algorithms can provide a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo methods when estimating a mean. A mean depends linearly on a probability distribution, so that result does not automatically settle what happens for nonlinear quantities. This paper asks whether the same scale of improvement is achievable for a broad nonlinear class called nested expectations.

The authors propose a quantum-inside-quantum algorithm that achieves the quadratic speedup for this class. Its central contribution is a new sequence of multilevel Monte Carlo approximations designed specifically for quantum computation. That construction improves on directly applying an existing quantum-accelerated multilevel Monte Carlo algorithm to the problem.

An existing lower bound shows that the proposed algorithm is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. This means its complexity is close to the theoretical limit expressed by that bound, while leaving room for differences involving logarithmic factors. The contribution extends the reach of quantum Monte Carlo acceleration to nested nonlinear estimation; the stated result applies to that broad class rather than establishing a speedup for every nonlinear functional.
neurips-2025-quantum-speedup-of-non-line.tldr: A quantum-inside-quantum algorithm achieves a quadratic speedup for nested expectations and is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Distribution testing asks whether probability distributions have a specified property using samples rather than complete knowledge of the distributions. This paper studies those questions within algorithmic replicability, where stability of the testing outcome across independently sampled data is part of the objective. The main resource of interest is sample complexity: how much data a replicable test needs.

The authors develop new replicable algorithms for testing closeness and independence of discrete distributions. These tasks concern whether distributions are sufficiently similar and whether variables behave independently. Placing them in the replicability framework adds a requirement beyond ordinary property testing, so identifying suitable algorithms and their data requirements becomes a distinct theoretical problem.

The paper also introduces a method for proving sample-complexity lower bounds. Applied to uniformity and closeness testing, it gives near-optimal bounds on the data required by replicable procedures. The uniformity result resolves an open question from earlier work. Together, the algorithmic and lower-bound contributions help characterize both what replicable testing can achieve and the statistical cost it cannot avoid.
neurips-2025-replicable-distribution-tes.tldr: The paper develops replicable distribution tests and near-optimal sample-complexity lower bounds for uniformity and closeness testing.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets participants collaboratively train a model, but obtaining fair performance across participants remains difficult. This paper questions two common choices: treating all parameters as relevant to fairness and continually favoring weaker clients throughout training. The authors argue that redundant parameter updates can create conflict, while persistent protection can obstruct global optimization and worsen both performance and fairness.

Their solution adjusts the model and the aggregation of client updates. A masking and rescaling mechanism discards redundant parameters from fairness adjustment and emphasizes critical ones, aiming to preserve useful updates and reduce conflict. A dynamic aggregation strategy then changes client weights using local update directions and variations in performance.

The client weighting is motivated by the observation that federated training has different characteristics at different stages. Fairness interventions therefore adapt as training progresses rather than applying the same protection throughout. Experiments in single-domain and cross-domain settings support the strategy's effectiveness and the efficiency of its key modules, providing empirical evidence for considering parameter relevance and training phase together.
neurips-2025-rethinking-fair-federated-l.tldr: Selective parameter adjustment and adaptive client weighting improve fair federated learning by addressing update conflicts and changing training needs.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization uses supervision from a weaker model to guide a more capable one. Although this can transfer knowledge on clean examples, the paper argues that it typically does not transfer adversarial robustness. Adversarial samples are usually absent during alignment, leaving stronger vision-language models vulnerable despite successful alignment on ordinary inputs.

The authors propose an unsupervised method for transferring robustness from weak to strong models and eliciting zero-shot robustness in large models. It addresses unreliable alignment information through two components: reweighting the alignment and refining the source guidance. These components focus on the supervision signal itself, which is central when the guiding model is less capable than the model being aligned.

The paper analyzes settings in which robustness generalization is possible, so its theoretical claim is conditional rather than universal. Experiments across several vision-language benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness in numerous scenarios and support plug-and-play use with large models. The contribution extends the weak-to-strong question from transferring clean-task knowledge to transferring resistance against adversarial inputs.
neurips-2025-robust-superalignment-weak-.tldr: An unsupervised weak-to-strong alignment method transfers adversarial robustness through alignment reweighting and refined source guidance.

paragraphs: SHAP values assign credit to input features for a model's individual predictions. Computing these explanations efficiently is the focus of this paper, which proposes a two-stage method for black-box predictors and tree models. The approach separates building a reusable model representation from calculating feature attributions for particular predictions.

First, the method expresses the predictor using a compact Fourier representation, motivated by spectral bias in real-world models. This representation is exact for trees and approximate for black-box predictors. Second, a closed-form formula computes SHAP values exactly from the Fourier representation through a simple summation that can be parallelized.

The distinction between the two stages matters for accuracy: an exact attribution calculation on an approximate black-box representation does not make the representation itself exact. Because the Fourier representation is computed once and reused, its initial cost can be spread over many explanations. The authors report significant speedups over existing methods and a tunable balance between efficiency and precision, making repeated attribution computation the main practical beneficiary.
neurips-2025-shap-values-via-sparse-four.tldr: A reusable sparse Fourier representation enables fast SHAP computation, with exact attribution summation and a tunable approximation trade-off for black-box models.

paragraphs: Fair classifiers need representations that remain useful for prediction while carrying little sensitive information. Existing approaches often rely on adversarial learning or matching distributions across sensitive groups. This paper targets the instability of adversarial training and the computational expense of distribution matching by using a distance based on characteristic functions.

The proposed objective uses that distance to minimize sensitive information in the learned representation while preserving downstream predictive effectiveness. The authors present it as a more stable and efficient approach than traditional alternatives. They also introduce a simple relaxation of the objective that guarantees fairness without performance degradation for common classification models, with the guarantee scoped to those models.

On benchmark datasets, the method consistently matches or improves on existing approaches in both fairness and predictive accuracy. The experiments also support its robustness and computational efficiency. The practical significance is the combination of a representation-learning objective with a simpler classifier-oriented relaxation: the paper seeks fairness improvements that remain compatible with useful prediction and manageable training costs.
neurips-2025-simple-and-effective-specia.tldr: Characteristic-function-based representation learning improves fairness and accuracy in benchmarks, with a relaxed objective guaranteeing fairness without performance loss for common classifiers.

paragraphs: Restless bandits model repeated choices whose expected rewards change over time. This paper studies two structured cases: rising rewards, which never decrease, and rising concave rewards, whose growth also slows. The question is how much cumulative regret a learning algorithm must incur when these changing reward functions are unknown.

The authors develop a lower-bound methodology and show that rising bandits require regret of at least order T^(2/3), matching known upper bounds for restless bandits. For rising concave bandits, they establish a lower bound of order T^(3/5). This proves that even the additional concavity structure leaves the problem statistically harder than stationary bandits.

They also introduce Rising Concave Budgeted Exploration, RC-BE(α), and prove an upper regret bound of order T^(7/11), up to logarithmic factors. The lower and upper exponents do not coincide, so a gap remains for the concave setting. Nevertheless, the results narrow that gap and place rising concave bandits between stationary and general restless problems in statistical complexity.
neurips-2025-tightening-regret-lower-and.tldr: New regret bounds and a rising-concave bandit algorithm narrow the complexity gap while proving this setting harder than stationary bandits.

paragraphs: A head-mounted camera captures details about a user's attention and hand-object interactions, but its narrow view can hide the larger scene. This creates difficulties for vision-language models answering spatial or contextual questions. The paper combines first-person and third-person images so that local interaction cues can be interpreted alongside global layout and broader object visibility.

The authors introduce E3VQA, a benchmark containing 4,000 question-answer pairs grounded in synchronized first-person and third-person image pairs. They also propose M3CoT, a prompting method that requires no additional training. It integrates scene graphs from three complementary perspectives into a unified scene representation to support reasoning across views.

Evaluations report consistent gains over a recent chain-of-thought baseline: 4.84% for GPT-4o and 5.94% for Gemini 2.0 Flash. The study also examines model strengths and limitations in multi-view reasoning. These results support both collecting complementary viewpoints and organizing their information explicitly, rather than assuming that a narrow first-person image contains enough context for demanding scene questions.
neurips-2025-towards-comprehensive-scene.tldr: E3VQA and the training-free M3CoT prompting method improve scene question answering by combining first-person and third-person visual context.

paragraphs: Adam is widely used with mini-batches, yet much theoretical analysis studies its full-batch version. This paper emphasizes that the distinction is fundamental: unlike stochastic gradient descent, stochastic Adam does not approach its full-batch counterpart merely by making the learning rate infinitesimal. Batch size therefore needs to be analyzed directly when explaining generalization.

The authors study two-layer, overparameterized convolutional neural networks on image data. In that setting, their theory shows that full-batch Adam and AdamW with proper weight decay converge to solutions with poor test error, while their mini-batch versions can achieve near-zero test error. The result identifies a substantial possible generalization difference within the analyzed model and data setting.

They also prove that Adam has a strictly smaller effective weight-decay bound than AdamW, explaining why Adam needs more sensitive tuning of the decay parameter. Extensive experiments validate the findings. Together, the analysis and experiments identify batch size and weight decay as interacting choices that matter for test performance, beyond whether the optimizer successfully fits the training problem.
neurips-2025-understanding-the-generaliz.tldr: Theory for overparameterized CNNs shows how mini-batching can improve Adam's generalization and why Adam requires more sensitive weight-decay tuning than AdamW.

paragraphs: Decentralized training can distribute a neural network across participants, each processing only part of it. Unextractable Protocol Models aim to keep that collaboration functional while preventing a usable complete weight set from being assembled across time. The framework periodically applies random, invertible transformations at participant boundaries, preserving the network's function while making shards from different time steps incompatible.

On Qwen-2.5-0.5B and Llama-3.2-1B, 10,000 transformations leave FP32 perplexity effectively unchanged, with reported changes below 0.01. Transforming every 30 seconds adds 3% inference latency, 0.1% bandwidth, and 10% GPU-memory overhead. During training, the reported overhead is 1.6% in time and less than 1% in memory. The authors also address controlling growth at lower precision.

The attack analysis finds direct attacks impractical under the considered conditions. Repairing stitched partitions through gradient-based fine-tuning consumes at least 60% of the tokens needed for training from scratch. These results support the framework's extraction resistance in the analyzed settings and its proposed use for embedding programmatic incentives in community-driven model training.
neurips-2025-unextractable-protocol-mode.tldr: UPMs preserve distributed model computation while making shards collected at different times incompatible, supporting extraction resistance with measured operational overhead.

paragraphs: Predicting where an enzyme cuts a protein can support drug development, enzyme design, and the study of biological mechanisms. Many existing predictors are built for a single enzyme. That separation leaves shared knowledge across enzymes unused and makes it difficult to extend predictions to enzymes the model has not previously encountered.

UniZyme addresses this problem with a unified cleavage-site predictor for diverse enzymes. Its architecture incorporates biochemical information and knowledge of proteolytic enzymes' active sites to strengthen how enzymes are represented. The aim is to make the enzyme description informative for cleavage prediction within one shared model, allowing knowledge to carry across enzyme identities.

Extensive experiments report high cleavage-site prediction accuracy across a range of proteolytic enzymes, including unseen enzymes. The unseen-enzyme result is especially relevant to the motivation: the model demonstrates generalization beyond the enzymes encountered during development. The findings support combining shared predictive modeling with enzyme-specific biochemical knowledge, while the demonstrated scope remains the range of enzymes covered by the experiments.
neurips-2025-unizyme-a-unified-protein-c.tldr: UniZyme combines a shared cleavage-site predictor with enzyme active-site knowledge to achieve high accuracy across diverse enzymes, including unseen ones.
